rubric.empty_rule: A mode that returns nothing scores 0. Silence is not precision.
rubric.rounding: Components are summed, then rounded to the nearest half point.

families.blurb: Exact terms, spelled the way the corpus spells them. The control group.
The question and the corpus use different words for the same thing, or the same word for different things.
A threshold or a field comparison wearing a nickname.
The answer is a count across records, which no single document states.
The absence of something. The known hard failure of dense retrieval.
Two or three translations that all have to land for the answer to be right.
A document asserts something the structured data contradicts.

caveats: Twelve questions is a demonstration, not a benchmark. Every one was written by the same person who wrote the corpus and the retrievers, which is the oldest way there is to build an eval that flatters your own system.
Relevance judgments are one person's opinion, applied consistently. They are published in full above each test so you can disagree with a specific one.
The rubric is arithmetic chosen to be legible, not a standard IR metric. Weighting the three components differently reorders the leaderboard.
Graph and ontology scores presume correct Cypher. In the live app that Cypher comes from a model and can be wrong; here it was written by hand.

tests.headline: Embeddings cannot represent 'not'
tests.preamble: A vector is a point in a space of topics, and 'conflict' and 'no conflict' land on the same point. Asking for the absence of something is the sharpest known failure of dense retrieval, and it is not a tuning problem - the representation has no slot for negation. This corpus makes it worse on purpose: one article's entire subject is a breakup in which nobody argued, and it embeds closer to 'conflict' than most of the real fights do.
tests.what_good_looks_like: Twenty-seven players who carry no conflict edge. Any article at all in the top three is a failed answer, because the question is about players and every article in that neighbourhood is about conflict.

steps.label: 1. Keyword leg (BM25)
steps.code:
SELECT d.doc_rowid, d.id, d.kind, d.ref_id, d.title, d.body, d.meta,
       bm25(documents_fts, 2.0, 1.0)                      AS bm25_score,
       snippet(documents_fts, 1, '[', ']', ' … ', 14)     AS excerpt
FROM documents_fts
JOIN documents AS d ON d.doc_rowid = documents_fts.rowid
WHERE documents_fts MATCH :match_expression
ORDER BY bm25_score          -- FTS5 returns BM25 negated, so ascending is best-first
LIMIT :limit
steps.note: BM25 scores come back negative from FTS5 (more negative is a better match), which is why the ORDER BY is ascending.

steps.label: Embed the rewritten query
steps.code:
model = TextEmbedding("BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5")
# bge models take an instruction prefix on the query side only
query_vector = next(model.query_embed([
    'Two players who used to be teammates and now play for different franchises.'
]))
# -> float32[384], L2-normalised
steps.note: The whole corpus was embedded once at startup with the same model. Only this one vector is computed per query.

steps.label: 2. Vector leg (cosine KNN)
steps.code:
SELECT d.id, d.kind, d.ref_id, d.title, d.body, d.meta,
       vec_distance_cosine(v.embedding, :query_vector) AS distance
FROM doc_vectors AS v
JOIN documents AS d ON d.doc_rowid = v.doc_rowid
WHERE v.embedding MATCH :query_vector
  AND k = :k
ORDER BY distance
steps.note: Cosine distance over unit vectors. Every document in the corpus gets a score, so this always returns k results - including when nothing is actually relevant.

steps.label: 3. Graph leg (Cypher)
steps.code:
MATCH (a:Player)-[r:FORMER_TEAMMATE]->(b:Player)
RETURN DISTINCT a.id AS id, a.name AS name, b.name AS counterpart,
       r.team_id AS via_team, r.to_season AS last_season
ORDER BY last_season DESC
LIMIT 25
steps.note: Pattern matching, not ranking. Five of the relationship types traversed here were derived at build time and appear in no source file.

by_family.blurb: Exact terms, spelled the way the corpus spells them. The control group.
The question and the corpus use different words for the same thing, or the same word for different things.
A threshold or a field comparison wearing a nickname.
The answer is a count across records, which no single document states.
The absence of something. The known hard failure of dense retrieval.
Two or three translations that all have to land for the answer to be right.
A document asserts something the structured data contradicts.

findings.title: There is no best retrieval mode, only a best mode per question shape
findings.body: Hybrid leads on mean score (4.54/5) and Keyword trails it (1.38/5), and that ordering tells you almost nothing on its own. Keyword search scores 5.0/5 on the lexical control - matching the best result any mode achieved on it, at 0.4 ms against 126.8 ms - and averages 1.05/5 across the other 11 questions. A mean over a question mix somebody chose is a statement about the mix. Change it and you change the winner.

findings.title: Semantic search never returns nothing, which is exactly the problem
findings.body: The vector leg returned a full page of 8 ranked results on every one of the 12 questions, including the 8 where it scored 1.5/5 or below. There is no similarity floor and no abstention: cosine distance always produces an ordering, so a question this corpus cannot answer looks exactly like one it can. Keyword search returned nothing on 1 question in the same suite. That is a worse experience and strictly better information.

findings.title: Traps are eaten by whoever matches on surface features
findings.body: This suite designates 12 documents as traps: wrong for the question, and tempting to one specific failure mode. Across the suite Keyword retrieved 7 of them and Semantic retrieved 4; Graph retrieved none. A trap only works if the retriever is matching something the document has and the answer does not: a shared string, a shared topic, a plausible headline. Modes that match against modelled structure cannot be fooled by prose, because they never read any.

findings.title: Fusion inherits its best leg, and its worst
findings.body: On the negation question keyword scored 0.5/5 and semantic 1.0/5 - both answered a question about the absence of conflict with documents about conflict. Hybrid scored 5.0/5 anyway, because the graph leg used NOT EXISTS and RRF weights it 2.5x, which was enough to outvote two legs agreeing with each other and not with the question. Then hybrid + ontology scored 0.5/5 on the identical question, because the expansion recognised 'conflict' as a modelled class and rewrote the graph leg into a CONFLICT_WITH traversal - turning the one leg that was right into the one that was most confidently wrong. Fusion did not detect anything in either direction. It counted votes.

findings.title: The ontology beats text retrieval comfortably and never beat plain hybrid here
findings.body: Against the text modes the case is emphatic: hybrid + ontology averages 3.96/5 against 1.83/5 for semantic, a gap of 2.13 points. Against plain hybrid it is not: across 12 questions 0 improved, 9 were unchanged and 3 got worse (showcase-two-hop, negation, two-defined-classes). Two things are going on and only one of them is about ontologies. The expansion widens the keyword and vector legs with class synonyms, which costs precision when the widened terms match a trap. And this suite pins the plan, which hands plain hybrid a hand-written Cypher that already encodes the very translations the ontology exists to derive. That is a real limitation of the experiment rather than a result: run it with --live-planner and the comparison is against Cypher a model wrote, which is the comparison that actually matters in production. What holds either way is the cost side - hybrid + ontology is the slowest mode in the suite at 144.2 ms median.

findings.title: Writing the judgments found three places where the prose and the records disagree
findings.body: Grading against ground truth rather than against output surfaced contradictions inside the corpus itself. One article is titled 'He was traded twice before he turned twenty-six'; the trade ledger records one trade for that player. Another is titled 'Two former teammates meet in the conference finals'; neither player carries a FORMER_TEAMMATE edge, because their season ranges never overlap. A third names six players from one college and the database holds eight, which is why keyword search scores 2.0/5 there while looking entirely successful. Every text mode believes all three, because believing the document is the only thing a text mode does. None of this was planted; it was in the corpus before the report existed and nothing in the app surfaced it. That is the actual argument for writing an eval.

findings.title: A mode's ceiling is set by the schema, not only by the technique
findings.body: Graph search scored 1.5/5 on the draft-pick question - its worst result in the suite - and the technique is not at fault. Draft picks were modelled as rows on a relational table rather than as nodes and edges, so there is nothing to traverse and the best available Cypher counts trades instead. No mode cleared 2.0/5 on it. The same question expressed as SQL over trade_picks is four lines. It is left in the report on purpose: modelling decisions made long before any query ran set the ceiling on what retrieval over that data can do, and a benchmark that quietly routes around its own schema gaps is measuring its author rather than the system.

findings.title: Failure has a different shape in each mode
findings.body: Keyword has the widest spread in the suite (0.0 to 5.0), but spread is the less interesting half. The text modes fail gradually: a slightly wrong page, ranked confidently, with a plausible top result. Graph search fails discontinuously - the Cypher either describes the question or it does not, and its floor in this suite is 1.5/5, on 'who owes the most unprotected first round picks?'. Pattern matching has no partial credit, which is a virtue when a wrong answer is expensive and a liability when any answer beats none. Note too that every graph and ontology score here presumes correct Cypher, which was written by hand; in the live app a model writes it and can be wrong in ways this report does not measure.
